lessonTitle: Abdominal Incisions and the Layers of the Wall

blocks.text: Two patients need laparotomy on the same morning. One has a long vertical scar down the midline, finished in minutes. The other has a low curved scar hidden in the bikini line. Both surgeons reached the peritoneum, but they crossed different layers and paid different prices in speed, access and later hernia risk.

blocks.markdown: An abdominal incision is a controlled journey through the **anterior abdominal wall**. Knowing the layers tells you what you will cut, what bleeds, what must be closed, and which nerves lie in your path. Away from the midline, the wall is a sandwich of three flat muscles whose fibres run in different directions, so the wall is strong and can be split rather than cut.

blocks.title: Anterior abdominal wall layers
blocks.text: From superficial to deep: skin; superficial fascia (fatty Camper's fascia and membranous Scarpa's fascia); external oblique; internal oblique; transversus abdominis; transversalis fascia; extraperitoneal fat; parietal peritoneum. Over the midline the central structure is the rectus abdominis muscle in its sheath, and the linea alba is the fibrous median raphe formed where the aponeuroses of the two sides meet.

blocks.markdown: The **rectus sheath** encloses the rectus abdominis. Above the arcuate line, the anterior wall of the sheath is the external oblique aponeurosis plus the anterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis; the posterior wall is the posterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis plus the transversus abdominis aponeurosis. Below the arcuate line (roughly midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis) all three aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus, so the muscle lies directly on transversalis fascia posteriorly.

rows: Fast, little bleeding, excellent access, easily extended
Linea alba is poorly vascularised, slower healing, higher incisional hernia risk
Vertical about 2 to 3 cm lateral to midline; rectus retracted laterally
Rectus muscle lies over the closed posterior sheath, giving a stronger closure
Slower and more complex; longer operating time
Curved transverse suprapubic, following skin tension lines
Good cosmesis, low hernia rate, strong closure
Limited access and extension, mainly pelvic organs
blocks.caption: Common abdominal incisions compared.

blocks.title: Layers crossed in a lower midline incision
blocks.prompt: Trace the layers a scalpel and then dissection cross in a midline incision placed 4 cm below the umbilicus to enter the peritoneal cavity.

steps.text: Skin and superficial fascia: Camper's fat then Scarpa's fascia are cut in the midline.
The incision lies over the linea alba, so the two rectus muscles are separated rather than cut; below the arcuate line there is no posterior rectus sheath.
Beneath the linea alba lie the transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and finally the parietal peritoneum.
No muscle fibres are divided, which explains why the incision is quick and bloodless but depends on the strength of the linea alba for closure.

blocks.answer: Skin, Camper's fascia, Scarpa's fascia, linea alba, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.

blocks.markdown: **Nerves.** The muscles and skin are supplied segmentally by the anterior rami of T7 to T11 (thoracoabdominal nerves), T12 (subcostal nerve) and L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves). They run forward in the plane **between internal oblique and transversus abdominis**, then pierce the rectus sheath at its lateral border to supply the rectus. A midline or transverse incision divides only small cutaneous branches because adjacent segments overlap. A vertical incision placed **lateral** to the rectus can divide several segmental nerves and leave part of the rectus paralysed and weak, predisposing to bulging and hernia.

**Vessels.** The superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic) and the inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac) run on the deep surface of the rectus within the sheath and anastomose near the umbilicus. They can bleed when the rectus is divided or retracted. Venous drainage runs with the arteries; the segmental arteries accompany the nerves.

blocks.title: Choosing a placement for a gallbladder approach
blocks.prompt: A surgeon plans a right subcostal incision about 3 cm below and parallel to the costal margin. Explain why this orientation is chosen and what a vertical extension lateral to the rectus would risk.

steps.text: The incision runs roughly parallel to the course of the segmental nerves T8 to T11 as they pass down and forward, so few nerves are cut across.
The rectus abdominis is divided and so are the superior epigastric vessels, which must be ligated.
A vertical extension lateral to the rectus would cut across several segmental nerves, leaving the muscle medial to it denervated and weak, so the long-term risk is bulge and incisional hernia.

blocks.answer: Subcostal incisions follow the nerves and spare most segmental supply; lateral vertical extensions risk denervation of the rectus.

blocks.title: Direction decides damage
blocks.text: Incisions that run parallel to segmental nerves and skin tension lines spare nerves and heal with better strength; incisions that cross nerves risk denervating the muscle between the cut and the midline.

blocks.title: Incision choice is a trade-off
blocks.text: No incision is best for every patient. Midline gives speed and access; transverse gives strength and cosmesis; paramedian gives a strong closure at the cost of time. The choice depends on the organ, urgency and patient.

points: Layers from skin to peritoneum: skin, Camper's and Scarpa's fascia, three flat muscles or their aponeuroses, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.

Midline incisions are fast and bloodless through the linea alba but closure relies on a poorly vascularised structure; paramedian incisions give a stronger closure; transverse incisions follow skin tension lines but limit access.
Segmental nerves T7 to L1 run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis and enter the rectus laterally; the epigastric arteries lie behind the rectus.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of layers from superficial to deep in the lateral abdominal wall (outside the rectus sheath)?

options.text: External oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia
Internal oblique, external oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia
Transversus abdominis, internal oblique, external oblique, transversalis fascia
External oblique, transversus abdominis, internal oblique, transversalis fascia

questions.correctOptionText: External oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: external oblique, then internal oblique, then transversus abdominis, then transversalis fascia.
distractorRationale.b: The internal oblique lies deep to the external oblique.
distractorRationale.c: The transversus abdominis is the deepest muscle layer.
distractorRationale.d: Transversus abdominis lies deep to internal oblique, not between external and internal oblique.

questions.explanation: The three flat muscles are layered external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis from superficial to deep, and the transversalis fascia lies deep to them. This order defines the plane in which segmental nerves run.

questions.stem: A surgeon opens the abdomen in the midline 5 cm below the umbilicus. Which structure forms the posterior covering of the rectus abdominis at this level?

options.text: Transversalis fascia only
Posterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis
External oblique aponeurosis
Linea alba

distractorRationale.a: Correct: below the arcuate line the aponeuroses all pass anterior to the rectus.
distractorRationale.b: The posterior lamina contributes to the sheath only above the arcuate line.
distractorRationale.c: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall.
distractorRationale.d: The linea alba is the midline raphe, not a posterior covering of the muscle.

questions.explanation: Below the arcuate line all three flat muscle aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus, leaving only transversalis fascia behind. This is why the sheath is weaker at low levels.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is scheduled for a Pfannenstiel incision for pelvic surgery. What is the main advantage compared with a midline incision?

options.text: Lower incisional hernia rate and a better cosmetic scar
Better access to the upper abdomen
No need to close the rectus sheath
It avoids all abdominal wall nerves

questions.correctOptionText: Lower incisional hernia rate and a better cosmetic scar

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it follows skin tension lines, giving good cosmesis and a strong closure.
distractorRationale.b: Access to the upper abdomen is limited, not better.
distractorRationale.c: The sheath is incised and must be closed.
distractorRationale.d: Small cutaneous branches may still be divided.

questions.explanation: A low transverse incision follows tension lines and has a lower hernia rate, though it provides limited access and extension. These are the trade-offs between transverse and midline incisions.

questions.stem: Which statement about the paramedian incision is correct?

options.text: Closure is stronger because the rectus muscle lies over the closed posterior sheath
It avoids dividing the skin
It is the fastest incision to make
It is placed through the linea alba

questions.correctOptionText: Closure is stronger because the rectus muscle lies over the closed posterior sheath

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the retracted rectus falls back over the posterior sheath closure.
distractorRationale.c: It is slower than a midline incision.
distractorRationale.d: Linea alba incision is midline; paramedian is lateral to it.

questions.explanation: In a paramedian incision the rectus is retracted laterally and then returns to cover the closure, which strengthens it. The cost is longer operating time and more dissection.

questions.stem: A midline incision through the linea alba divides few muscle fibres and little vascular tissue, which is why it bleeds little.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The linea alba is a fibrous, poorly vascularised raphe between the two recti. Because it is an aponeurotic structure, the incision splits the muscles apart rather than cutting through them, which minimises bleeding.

questions.stem: A surgeon makes a long vertical incision through the muscles of the lateral abdominal wall, lateral to the border of the rectus abdominis. Which late complication is most associated with this?

options.text: Weakness and bulge of the rectus muscle medial to the incision due to denervation
Loss of sensation over the shoulder
Injury to the thoracic duct
Paralysis of the diaphragm

questions.correctOptionText: Weakness and bulge of the rectus muscle medial to the incision due to denervation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: segmental nerves enter the rectus laterally and are cut by lateral vertical incisions.
distractorRationale.b: Shoulder sensation is not supplied by the abdominal wall nerves.
distractorRationale.c: The thoracic duct is not at risk in the abdominal wall.
distractorRationale.d: The diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve.

questions.explanation: Segmental nerves run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis and enter the rectus at its lateral border. A vertical cut lateral to the rectus can divide them, leaving the medial rectus denervated and prone to bulge.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a transverse incision across the rectus sheath. Which vessel pair lies on the deep surface of the rectus and may need to be ligated?

options.text: Superior and inferior epigastric arteries
Internal and external pudendal arteries
Superficial circumflex iliac and superficial epigastric arteries
Intercostal and lumbar arteries only

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the epigastric arteries run on the deep surface of the rectus in the sheath.
distractorRationale.c: Superficial arteries lie in the subcutaneous layer.
distractorRationale.d: Intercostal and lumbar arteries accompany the nerves, not the rectus deep surface.

questions.explanation: The superior epigastric (from the internal thoracic) and the inferior epigastric (from the external iliac) arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath. They run behind the rectus and bleed if it is divided.

questions.stem: List the layers an incision crosses from skin to peritoneum in the midline above the arcuate line, and explain why a midline incision is quick but has a higher hernia risk.
markingGuide: Skin and superficial fascia (Camper's and Scarpa's).
Transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.
No muscle fibres are cut so it is quick and bloodless.
Linea alba is poorly vascularised and heals slowly, risking incisional hernia.
questions.explanation: In the midline the aponeuroses fuse into the linea alba, so the path is short and avascular. Closure depends on a poorly vascularised fibrous structure, which heals slowly and may fail under tension.

questions.stem: Explain how the course of the segmental nerves influences where an abdominal incision should be placed, and why a transverse incision is generally tolerated.
markingGuide: Segmental nerves (T7 to L1) run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
They enter the rectus sheath at the lateral border of the rectus.
Incisions parallel to the nerve course or in the midline cut few nerves.
Lateral vertical incisions risk denervation of the rectus medial to the cut.
Overlap of dermatomes and small cutaneous branches means transverse incisions are tolerated.
questions.explanation: The pathways of the nerves dictate which cuts are safe. Orientation that follows or avoids their course spares muscle innervation, whereas cuts across several adjacent nerves can leave a muscle segment paralysed.

questions.stem: A surgeon compares a midline incision with a paramedian incision for a long operation. Discuss the trade-offs.
markingGuide: Midline is faster and gives wide access and easy extension.
Midline closure depends on the poorly vascularised linea alba, increasing hernia risk.
Paramedian incision stronger closure because rectus covers posterior sheath.
Paramedian incision slower, longer operating time.
Choice depends on urgency, organ and patient.
questions.explanation: Speed, access, strength and healing are traded against one another. Urgent cases usually favour midline; elective cases where closure strength matters may favour paramedian.
